bbccf52c9c4871a54f19.caption: Notice that the crystals of sodium chloride dissociate not into molecules of NaCl, but into Na + cations and Cl – anions, each completely surrounded by water molecules.
bbccf52c9c4871a54f19.alt: This figure shows a crystal lattice of sodium chloride interacting with water to form a hydrated sodium ion and a hydrated chloride ion.
bbccf52c9c4871a54f19.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

e7a066239695b4c6a514.title: Elements of the Human Body
e7a066239695b4c6a514.caption: The main elements that compose the human body are shown from most abundant to least abundant.
e7a066239695b4c6a514.alt: This figure shows a human body with the percentage of the main elements in the body, in the left panel. In the right panel, a table lists the elements and the percentages in the body.
e7a066239695b4c6a514.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

c2fcf203c662ebbff617.title: Structure of an Amino Acid
c2fcf203c662ebbff617.alt: This figure shows the structure of an amino acid.
c2fcf203c662ebbff617.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

a9a16fb839235ef6be35.title: Composition of Blood
a9a16fb839235ef6be35.caption: The cellular elements of blood include a vast number of erythrocytes and comparatively fewer leukocytes and platelets. Plasma is the fluid in which the formed elements are suspended. A sample of blood spun in a centrifuge reveals that plasma is the lightest component. It floats at the top of the tube separated from the heaviest elements, the erythrocytes, by a buffy coat of leukocytes and platelets. Hematocrit is the percentage of the total sample that is comprised of erythrocytes. Depressed and elevated hematocrit levels are shown for comparison.
a9a16fb839235ef6be35.alt: This figure shows three test tubes with a red and yellow liquid in them. The left panel shows normal blood, the center panel shows anemic blood and the right panel shows polycythemic blood.
a9a16fb839235ef6be35.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

8500ebba83b8528c480c.title: Summary of Formed Elements in Blood
8500ebba83b8528c480c.alt: This table shows the different types of cells present in blood, the number of cells, their appearance, and a summary of their function.
8500ebba83b8528c480c.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

6baea94fa24d02395f6f.title: Hemoglobin
6baea94fa24d02395f6f.caption: (a) A molecule of hemoglobin contains four globin proteins, each of which is bound to one molecule of the iron-containing pigment heme. (b) A single erythrocyte can contain 300 million hemoglobin molecules, and thus more than 1 billion oxygen molecules.
6baea94fa24d02395f6f.alt: This figure shows the structure of hemoglobin. The left panel shows the protein structure and the right panel shows the chemical formula.
6baea94fa24d02395f6f.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

0b9040bac5bbb3d67a50.title: Hematopoietic System of Bone Marrow
0b9040bac5bbb3d67a50.caption: Hemopoiesis is the proliferation and differentiation of the formed elements of blood.
0b9040bac5bbb3d67a50.alt: This flowchart shows the pathways in which a multipotent hemotopoietic stem cell differentiates into the different cell types found in blood.
0b9040bac5bbb3d67a50.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

76c3d1f710bcb00353ff.title: Erythrocyte Lifecycle
76c3d1f710bcb00353ff.caption: Erythrocytes are produced in the bone marrow and sent into the circulation. At the end of their lifecycle, they are destroyed by macrophages, and their components are recycled.
76c3d1f710bcb00353ff.alt: This flow chart shows the life cycle of a red blood cell. The first step is the hemopoeisis of erythrocytes in the bone marrow. Further steps in this diagram show the passage of erythrocytes through the blood stream, the breakdown of heme protein, and liver function.
76c3d1f710bcb00353ff.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

5a1ac9b3b7133e11a2a0.title: Erythroblastosis Fetalis
5a1ac9b3b7133e11a2a0.caption: The first exposure of an Rh − person to Rh + erythrocytes during pregnancy induces sensitization. Anti-Rh antibodies begin to circulate in the pregnant person's bloodstream. A second exposure occurs with a subsequent pregnancy with an Rh + fetus in the uterus. During that subsequent pregnancy, the pregnant person's anti-Rh antibodies may cross the placenta and enter the fetal bloodstream, causing agglutination and hemolysis of fetal erythrocytes.
5a1ac9b3b7133e11a2a0.alt: This figure shows an umbilical artery and vein passing through the placenta on the top left. The top right panel shows the first exposure to Rh+ antibodies in the mother. The bottom right panel shows the response when the second exposure in the form of another fetus takes place. Textboxes detail the steps in each process.
5a1ac9b3b7133e11a2a0.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

20df7980bfe626dfd39f.title: Granular Leukocytes
20df7980bfe626dfd39f.caption: A neutrophil has small granules that stain light lilac and a nucleus with two to five lobes. An eosinophil’s granules are slightly larger and stain reddish-orange, and its nucleus has two to three lobes. A basophil has large granules that stain dark blue to purple and a two-lobed nucleus.
20df7980bfe626dfd39f.alt: The  left image shows a neutrophil, the middle image shows an eosinophil, and the right image shows a basophil.
20df7980bfe626dfd39f.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

9e45c9f210abc0982d53.title: Platelets
9e45c9f210abc0982d53.caption: Platelets are derived from cells called megakaryocytes.
9e45c9f210abc0982d53.alt: This flowchart shows a myeloid stem cell differentiating into platelets.
9e45c9f210abc0982d53.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

8aaba912079b7b10655f.title: Hemostasis
8aaba912079b7b10655f.caption: (a) An injury to a blood vessel initiates the process of hemostasis. Blood clotting involves three steps. First, vascular spasm constricts the flow of blood. Next, a platelet plug forms to temporarily seal small openings in the vessel. Coagulation then enables the repair of the vessel wall once the leakage of blood has stopped. (b) The synthesis of fibrin in blood clots involves either an intrinsic pathway or an extrinsic pathway, both of which lead to a common pathway. (credit a: Kevin MacKenzie)
8aaba912079b7b10655f.alt: This figure details the steps in the clotting of blood. Each step is shown along with a detailed text box describing the steps on the left. On the right, a signaling pathway shows the different chemical signals involved in the clotting process.
8aaba912079b7b10655f.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

7d87327b2fa6f40d18fb.title: ABO Blood Group
7d87327b2fa6f40d18fb.caption: This chart summarizes the characteristics of the blood types in the ABO blood group. See the text for more on the concept of a universal donor or recipient.
7d87327b2fa6f40d18fb.alt: This table shows the different blood types, the antibodies in plasma, the antigens in the red blood cell, and the blood compatible blood types in an emergency.
7d87327b2fa6f40d18fb.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

4057d6efede4f9c9daef.title: Cross Matching Blood Types
4057d6efede4f9c9daef.caption: This sample of a commercially produced “bedside” card enables quick typing of both a recipient’s and donor’s blood before transfusion. The card contains three reaction sites or wells. One is coated with an anti-A antibody, one with an anti-B antibody, and one with an anti-D antibody (tests for the presence of Rh factor D). Mixing a drop of blood and saline into each well enables the blood to interact with a preparation of type-specific antibodies, also called anti-seras. Agglutination of RBCs in a given site indicates a positive identification of the blood antigens, in this case A and Rh antigens for blood type A + . For the purpose of transfusion, the donor’s and recipient’s blood types must match.
4057d6efede4f9c9daef.alt: This figure shows three different red blood cells with different blood types.
4057d6efede4f9c9daef.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

3435efc3042e3fc4a19d.title: Distribution of Blood Flow
3435efc3042e3fc4a19d.alt: This table describes the distribution of blood flow. 84 percent of blood flow is systemic circulation, of which 64 percent happens in systemic veins (18 percent in large veins, 21 percent in large venous networks such as liver, bone marrow, and integument, and 25 percent in venules and medium-sized veins); 13 percent happens in systemic arteries (2 percent in arterioles, 5 percent in muscular arteries, 4 percent in elastic arteries, and 2 percent in the aorta); and 7 percent happens in systemic capillaries. 9 percent of blood flow is pulmonary circulation, of which 4 percent happens in pulmonary veins, 2 percent happens in pulmonary capillaries, and 3 percent happens in pulmonary arteries. The remaining 7 percent of blood flow is in the heart.
3435efc3042e3fc4a19d.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

316a14d94e4ae9211bed.title: Relationships among Vessels in the Systemic Circuit
316a14d94e4ae9211bed.caption: The relationships among blood vessels that can be compared include (a) vessel diameter, (b) total cross-sectional area, (c) average blood pressure, and (d) velocity of blood flow.
316a14d94e4ae9211bed.alt: This figure shows four graphs. The top left graph shows the vessel diameter for different types of blood vessels. The top right panel shows cross-sectional area for different blood vessels. The bottom left panel shows the average blood pressure for different blood vessels, and the bottom right panel shows the velocity of blood flow in different blood vessels.
316a14d94e4ae9211bed.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

9b454749928054b833b4.title: Hepatic Portal System
9b454749928054b833b4.caption: The liver receives blood from the normal systemic circulation via the hepatic artery. It also receives and processes blood from other organs, delivered via the veins of the hepatic portal system. All blood exits the liver via the hepatic vein, which delivers the blood to the inferior vena cava. (Different colors are used to help distinguish among the different vessels in the system.)
9b454749928054b833b4.alt: This diagram shows the veins in the digestive system.
9b454749928054b833b4.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

4623845048f273033c21.title: Summary of Mechanisms Regulating Arteriole Smooth Muscle and Veins
4623845048f273033c21.alt: This table summarizes mechanisms that regulate arteriole smooth muscle and veins. Neural controls are regulated by sympathetic stimulation and parasympathetic. Endocrine controls are regulated by epinephrine, norepinephrine, angiotensin II, ANH (peptide), and ADH. Other factors include decreasing levels of oxygen, decreasing pH, increasing levels of carbon dioxide, increasing levels of potassium ion, increasing levels of prostaglandins, increasing levels of andenosine, increasing levels of NO, increasing levels of lactic acid and other metabolites, increasing levels of endothelins, increasing levels of platelet secretions, increasing hyperhtermia, stretching of vascular wall (myogenic), and increasing levels of histamines from basophils and mast cells.
4623845048f273033c21.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

90ef0936c2776c3850fc.title: Veins of the Thoracic and Abdominal Regions
90ef0936c2776c3850fc.caption: Veins of the thoracic and abdominal regions drain blood from the area above the diaphragm, returning it to the right atrium via the superior vena cava.
90ef0936c2776c3850fc.alt: This diagram shows the veins present in the thoracic abdominal cavity.
90ef0936c2776c3850fc.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

cd0093b9d67aef993dad.title: Capillary Bed
cd0093b9d67aef993dad.caption: In a capillary bed, arterioles give rise to metarterioles. Precapillary sphincters located at the junction of a metarteriole with a capillary regulate blood flow. A thoroughfare channel connects the metarteriole to a venule. An arteriovenous anastomosis, which directly connects the arteriole with the venule, is shown at the bottom.
cd0093b9d67aef993dad.alt: This diagram shows a capillary bed connecting an arteriole and a venule.
cd0093b9d67aef993dad.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

496d595300b1882a4bdc.title: Comparison of Veins and Venules
496d595300b1882a4bdc.caption: Many veins have valves to prevent back flow of blood, whereas venules do not. In terms of scale, the diameter of a venule is measured in micrometers compared to millimeters for veins.
496d595300b1882a4bdc.alt: The top panel shows the cross-section of a large vein, the middle panel shows the cross-section of a medium sized vein, and the bottom panel shows the cross-section of a venule.
496d595300b1882a4bdc.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

bee6b3f3d6a9b6e8b8be.title: Skeletal Muscle Pump
bee6b3f3d6a9b6e8b8be.caption: The contraction of skeletal muscles surrounding a vein compresses the blood and increases the pressure in that area. This action forces blood closer to the heart where venous pressure is lower. Note the importance of the one-way valves to assure that blood flows only in the proper direction.
bee6b3f3d6a9b6e8b8be.alt: The left panel shows the structure of a skeletal muscle vein pump when the muscle is relaxed, and the right panel shows the structure of a skeletal muscle vein pump when the muscle is contracted.
bee6b3f3d6a9b6e8b8be.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

0bb1685f55364eef7d03.title: Systemic Blood Pressure
0bb1685f55364eef7d03.caption: The graph shows the components of blood pressure throughout the blood vessels, including systolic, diastolic, mean arterial, and pulse pressures.
0bb1685f55364eef7d03.alt: This graph shows the value of pulse pressure in different types of blood vessels.
0bb1685f55364eef7d03.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

89c4f9a0be4761b405e4.title: Summary of Factors Maintaining Vascular Homeostasis
89c4f9a0be4761b405e4.caption: Adequate blood flow, blood pressure, distribution, and perfusion involve autoregulatory, neural, and endocrine mechanisms.
89c4f9a0be4761b405e4.alt: This flowchart shows the various factors that control the flow of blood. The top panel focuses on autoregulation, and the bottom panel focuses on neural and endocrine mechanisms.
89c4f9a0be4761b405e4.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

95a947b80a02c4599e5c.title: Pulse Sites
95a947b80a02c4599e5c.caption: The pulse is most readily measured at the radial artery, but can be measured at any of the pulse points shown.
95a947b80a02c4599e5c.alt: This image shows the pulse points in a woman’s body.
95a947b80a02c4599e5c.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

b3e735db58ae41a6d48d.title: Homeostatic Responses to Loss of Blood Volume
b3e735db58ae41a6d48d.alt: This flowchart shows the action of decreased blood pressure and volume in the neural and endocrine mechanisms.
b3e735db58ae41a6d48d.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

875f6b63bc666dffc265.title: Pulmonary Circuit
875f6b63bc666dffc265.caption: Blood exiting from the right ventricle flows into the pulmonary trunk, which bifurcates into the two pulmonary arteries. These vessels branch to supply blood to the pulmonary capillaries, where gas exchange occurs within the lung alveoli. Blood returns via the pulmonary veins to the left atrium.
875f6b63bc666dffc265.alt: This diagram shows the network of blood vessels in the lungs.
875f6b63bc666dffc265.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

e2df29f547e6bce97152.title: Hormones Involved in Renal Control of Blood Pressure
e2df29f547e6bce97152.caption: In the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone mechanism, increasing angiotensin II will stimulate the production of antidiuretic hormone and aldosterone. In addition to renin, the kidneys produce erythropoietin, which stimulates the production of red blood cells, further increasing blood volume.
e2df29f547e6bce97152.alt: This flow chart shows the action of decreased blood pressure in the short and long term.
e2df29f547e6bce97152.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

b819dedbd6d3d0e8f511.title: Interaction of the Circulatory System with Other Body Systems
b819dedbd6d3d0e8f511.alt: This table outlines the role of the circulatory system in the other organ systems in the body.
b819dedbd6d3d0e8f511.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

fee81e05df7a52bbb8f0.title: Baroreceptor Reflexes for Maintaining Vascular Homeostasis
fee81e05df7a52bbb8f0.caption: Increased blood pressure results in increased rates of baroreceptor firing, whereas decreased blood pressure results in slower rates of fire, both initiating the homeostatic mechanism to restore blood pressure.
fee81e05df7a52bbb8f0.alt: This flow chart shows what happens when blood pressure is increased or decreased. The top panel shows the events that take place when blood pressure is increased, and the bottom panel shows the events that take place when blood pressure is decreased.
fee81e05df7a52bbb8f0.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

b9c276363855b0789427.title: Blood Pressure Measurement
b9c276363855b0789427.caption: When pressure in a sphygmomanometer cuff is released, a clinician can hear the Korotkoff sounds. In this graph, a blood pressure tracing is aligned to a measurement of systolic and diastolic pressures.
b9c276363855b0789427.alt: This image shows blood pressure as a function of time.
b9c276363855b0789427.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

8d59daf827ec5605819a.title: Aorta
8d59daf827ec5605819a.caption: The aorta has distinct regions, including the ascending aorta, aortic arch, and the descending aorta, which includes the thoracic and abdominal regions.
8d59daf827ec5605819a.alt: This diagram shows the aorta and the major parts are labeled.
8d59daf827ec5605819a.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

9866779ec1978db52a10.title: Arteries Supplying the Head and Neck
9866779ec1978db52a10.caption: The common carotid artery gives rise to the external and internal carotid arteries. The external carotid artery remains superficial and gives rise to many arteries of the head. The internal carotid artery first forms the carotid sinus and then reaches the brain via the carotid canal and carotid foramen, emerging into the cranium via the foramen lacerum. The vertebral artery branches from the subclavian artery and passes through the transverse foramen in the cervical vertebrae, entering the base of the skull at the vertebral foramen. The subclavian artery continues toward the arm as the axillary artery.
9866779ec1978db52a10.alt: This diagram shows the blood vessels in the head and brain.
9866779ec1978db52a10.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

e0162d0bc54edc96edaa.title: Arteries of the Thoracic and Abdominal Regions
e0162d0bc54edc96edaa.caption: The thoracic aorta gives rise to the arteries of the visceral and parietal branches.
e0162d0bc54edc96edaa.alt: This diagram shows the arteries in the thoracic and abdominal cavity.
e0162d0bc54edc96edaa.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

2416b5b34b02594803d5.title: Major Branches of the Iliac Arteries
2416b5b34b02594803d5.caption: The flow chart summarizes the distribution of the major branches of the common iliac arteries into the pelvis and lower limbs. The left side follows a similar pattern to the right.
2416b5b34b02594803d5.alt: This flowchart shows the different branches into which that the abdominal aorta is divided.
2416b5b34b02594803d5.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

9ffc7b05753c9cbd2978.title: Major Arteries Serving the Thorax and Upper Limb
9ffc7b05753c9cbd2978.caption: The arteries that supply blood to the arms and hands are extensions of the subclavian arteries.
9ffc7b05753c9cbd2978.alt: This diagram shows the arteries in the arm.
9ffc7b05753c9cbd2978.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

923ca6a39fd50f9095f6.title: Arteries Serving the Brain
923ca6a39fd50f9095f6.caption: This inferior view shows the network of arteries serving the brain. The structure is referred to as the arterial circle or circle of Willis.
923ca6a39fd50f9095f6.alt: This diagram shows the arteries of the brain.
923ca6a39fd50f9095f6.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

ca75b166fa0dbf5b93fd.title: Veins Flowing into the Superior Vena Cava
ca75b166fa0dbf5b93fd.caption: The flow chart summarizes the distribution of the veins flowing into the superior vena cava.
ca75b166fa0dbf5b93fd.alt: This flowchart shows the different veins in the body, and how they are connected to the superior vena cava.
ca75b166fa0dbf5b93fd.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

76b2f8f70247f9b0fc4d.title: Venous Flow into Inferior Vena Cava
76b2f8f70247f9b0fc4d.caption: The flow chart summarizes veins that deliver blood to the inferior vena cava.
76b2f8f70247f9b0fc4d.alt: This chart shows the connection between the different veins and the inferior vena cava.
76b2f8f70247f9b0fc4d.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

aa894477da120b5ea72c.title: Veins of the Upper Limb
aa894477da120b5ea72c.caption: This anterior view shows the veins that drain the upper limb.
aa894477da120b5ea72c.alt: This diagram shows the veins present in the upper limb.
aa894477da120b5ea72c.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

7c45d2316241606ed626.title: Fetal Shunts
7c45d2316241606ed626.caption: The foramen ovale in the interatrial septum allows blood to flow from the right atrium to the left atrium. The ductus arteriosus is a temporary vessel, connecting the aorta to the pulmonary trunk. The ductus venosus links the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava largely through the liver.
7c45d2316241606ed626.alt: This figure shows the blood vessels in a fetus.
7c45d2316241606ed626.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

903de834121aab05836c.title: Cardiovascular Circulation
903de834121aab05836c.caption: The pulmonary circuit moves blood from the right side of the heart to the lungs and back to the heart. The systemic circuit moves blood from the left side of the heart to the head and body and returns it to the right side of the heart to repeat the cycle. The arrows indicate the direction of blood flow, and the colors show the relative levels of oxygen concentration.
903de834121aab05836c.alt: This diagram shows how oxygenated and deoxygenated blood flow through the major organs in the body.
903de834121aab05836c.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

139659292d03f58051be.title: Major Veins of the Lower Limb
139659292d03f58051be.caption: The flow chart summarizes venous flow from the lower limb.
139659292d03f58051be.alt: This charts shows the veins in the lower limbs, and how they are connected.
139659292d03f58051be.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

d2e6574c759e4ecdc23e.title: Capillary Exchange
d2e6574c759e4ecdc23e.caption: Net filtration occurs near the arterial end of the capillary since capillary hydrostatic pressure (CHP) is greater than blood colloidal osmotic pressure (BCOP). There is no net movement of fluid near the midpoint of the capillary since CHP = BCOP. Net reabsorption occurs near the venous end of the capillary since BCOP is greater than CHP.
d2e6574c759e4ecdc23e.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

340645db0e0213280e5a.title: Capillary Exchange
340645db0e0213280e5a.caption: Net filtration occurs near the arterial end of the capillary since capillary hydrostatic pressure (CHP) is greater than blood colloidal osmotic pressure (BCOP). There is no net movement of fluid near the midpoint since CHP = BCOP. Net reabsorption occurs near the venous end since BCOP is greater than CHP.
340645db0e0213280e5a.alt: This diagram shows the process of fluid exchange in a capillary from the arterial end to the venous end.
340645db0e0213280e5a.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

4f7b11dd3fad6737c8c5.title: Major Branches of the Aorta
4f7b11dd3fad6737c8c5.caption: The flow chart summarizes the distribution of the major branches of the aorta into the thoracic and abdominal regions.
4f7b11dd3fad6737c8c5.alt: This table shows the different arteries in the thoracic and abdominal cavity. The list on the left shows unpaired arteries, and the list on the right shows paired cavities.
4f7b11dd3fad6737c8c5.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

2f8aface2c2ae1937126.title: Systemic Arteries of the Lower Limb
2f8aface2c2ae1937126.caption: The flow chart summarizes the distribution of the systemic arteries from the external iliac artery into the lower limb.
2f8aface2c2ae1937126.alt: This chart shows the major arteries present in the lower limbs.
2f8aface2c2ae1937126.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

1d843bbb82ea185855a8.title: The Cerebrum
1d843bbb82ea185855a8.caption: The cerebrum is a large component of the CNS in humans, and the most obvious aspect of it is the folded surface called the cerebral cortex.
1d843bbb82ea185855a8.alt: This figure shows the lateral view on the left panel and anterior view on the right panel of the brain. The major parts including the cerebrum are labeled.
1d843bbb82ea185855a8.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

dcacfeb5c9193ff5d6df.title: Frontal Section of Cerebral Cortex and Basal Nuclei
dcacfeb5c9193ff5d6df.caption: The major components of the basal nuclei, shown in a frontal section of the brain, are the caudate (just lateral to the lateral ventricle), the putamen (inferior to the caudate and separated by the large white-matter structure called the internal capsule), and the globus pallidus (medial to the putamen).
dcacfeb5c9193ff5d6df.alt: This diagram shows the frontal section of the brain and identifies the major components of the basal nuclei.
dcacfeb5c9193ff5d6df.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

f512c1dc23da8c878c6e.title: Connections of Basal Nuclei
f512c1dc23da8c878c6e.caption: Input to the basal nuclei is from the cerebral cortex, which is an excitatory connection releasing glutamate as a neurotransmitter. This input is to the striatum, or the caudate and putamen. In the direct pathway, the striatum projects to the internal segment of the globus pallidus and the substantia nigra pars reticulata (GPi/SNr). This is an inhibitory pathway, in which GABA is released at the synapse, and the target cells are hyperpolarized and less likely to fire. The output from the basal nuclei is to the thalamus, which is an inhibitory projection using GABA. The diagram also includes the substantia nigra compacta (SNc), globus pallidus external segment (GPe), and subthalamic nucleus (STN).
f512c1dc23da8c878c6e.alt: This flowchart shows the connection between the different regions of the brain such as the cortex, striatum and the thalamus.
f512c1dc23da8c878c6e.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

50a6a75c25fda119b903.title: The Eye in the Orbit
50a6a75c25fda119b903.caption: The eye is located within the orbit and surrounded by soft tissues that protect and support its function. The orbit is surrounded by cranial bones of the skull.
50a6a75c25fda119b903.alt: This diagram shows the lateral view of the eye. The major parts are labeled.
50a6a75c25fda119b903.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

8ee2cf787cfc692c9a22.title: The Sensory Homunculus
8ee2cf787cfc692c9a22.caption: A cartoon representation of the sensory homunculus arranged adjacent to the cortical region in which the processing takes place.
8ee2cf787cfc692c9a22.alt: This image shows the areas of the brain that control and respond to the different senses.
8ee2cf787cfc692c9a22.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

86deaf348db729508568.title: Early Embryonic Development of Nervous System
86deaf348db729508568.caption: The neuroectoderm begins to fold inward to form the neural groove. As the two sides of the neural groove converge, they form the neural tube, which lies beneath the ectoderm. The anterior end of the neural tube will develop into the brain, and the posterior portion will become the spinal cord. The neural crest develops into peripheral structures.
86deaf348db729508568.alt: This figure shows the development of the neural tube in an embryo. The left panel shows the formation of a neural fold in the neuroectoderm. The middle panel shows the formation of the neural plate and the right panel shows the formation of the neural crest and neural tube.
86deaf348db729508568.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

a562a96882d8402f399e.title: Corticospinal Tract
a562a96882d8402f399e.caption: The major descending tract that controls skeletal muscle movements is the corticospinal tract. It is composed of two neurons, the upper motor neuron and the lower motor neuron. The upper motor neuron has its cell body in the primary motor cortex of the frontal lobe and synapses on the lower motor neuron, which is in the ventral horn of the spinal cord and projects to the skeletal muscle in the periphery.
a562a96882d8402f399e.alt: This diagram shows how the motor neurons thread their way through the spinal cord and into the brain. It also shows the different connections they make along the way.
a562a96882d8402f399e.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

c94c06b5bfbf1ce18d71.title: Lobes of the Cerebral Cortex
c94c06b5bfbf1ce18d71.caption: The cerebral cortex is divided into four lobes. Extensive folding increases the surface area available for cerebral functions.
c94c06b5bfbf1ce18d71.alt: This figure shows the lateral view of the brain and the major lobes are labeled.
c94c06b5bfbf1ce18d71.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

cf523efe1021a21438d9.title: Ventral and Dorsal Visual Streams
cf523efe1021a21438d9.caption: From the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe, visual processing continues in two streams—one into the temporal lobe and one into the parietal lobe.
cf523efe1021a21438d9.alt: This image shows the side of the human brain and maps different regions to different visual functions.
cf523efe1021a21438d9.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

aa2d22d6b2be1ca486fb.title: Phineas Gage
aa2d22d6b2be1ca486fb.caption: The victim of an accident while working on a railroad in 1848, Phineas Gage had a large iron rod impaled through the prefrontal cortex of his frontal lobe. After the accident, his personality appeared to change, but he eventually learned to cope with the trauma and lived as a coach driver even after such a traumatic event. (credit b: John M. Harlow, MD)
aa2d22d6b2be1ca486fb.alt: This photo shows Phineas Gage holding the metal spike that impaled his prefrontal cortex.
aa2d22d6b2be1ca486fb.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

d64f5ccd2b885e61ced2.title: The Diencephalon
d64f5ccd2b885e61ced2.caption: The diencephalon is composed primarily of the thalamus and hypothalamus, which together define the walls of the third ventricle. The thalami are two elongated, ovoid structures on either side of the midline that make contact in the middle. The hypothalamus is inferior and anterior to the thalamus, culminating in a sharp angle to which the pituitary gland is attached.
d64f5ccd2b885e61ced2.alt: This figure shows the location of the thalamus, hypothalamus and pituitary gland in the brain.
d64f5ccd2b885e61ced2.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

9da8c3dbbdb6240c923d.title: The Brain Stem
9da8c3dbbdb6240c923d.caption: The brain stem comprises three regions: the midbrain, the pons, and the medulla.
9da8c3dbbdb6240c923d.alt: This figure shows the location of the midbrain, pons and the medulla in the brain.
9da8c3dbbdb6240c923d.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

8e8c5d14d098828242c1.title: Meningeal Layers of Superior Sagittal Sinus
8e8c5d14d098828242c1.caption: The layers of the meninges in the longitudinal fissure of the superior sagittal sinus are shown, with the dura mater adjacent to the inner surface of the cranium, the pia mater adjacent to the surface of the brain, and the arachnoid and subarachnoid space between them. An arachnoid villus is shown emerging into the dural sinus to allow CSF to filter back into the blood for drainage.
8e8c5d14d098828242c1.alt: This image shows a cross-section through the brain. The different meningeal layers are labeled.
8e8c5d14d098828242c1.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

e44a9dc042ff6f3da87e.title: Cerebrospinal Fluid Circulation
e44a9dc042ff6f3da87e.caption: The choroid plexus in the four ventricles produce CSF, which is circulated through the ventricular system and then enters the subarachnoid space through the median and lateral apertures. The CSF is then reabsorbed into the blood at the arachnoid granulations, where the arachnoid membrane emerges into the dural sinuses.
e44a9dc042ff6f3da87e.alt: This diagram shows the cross section of the brain and the major parts are labeled. Arrows on the figure show the direction of circulation of the cerebro-spinal fluid.
e44a9dc042ff6f3da87e.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

5b5d7b8ec12ba5c33733.title: Dural Sinuses and Veins
5b5d7b8ec12ba5c33733.caption: Blood drains from the brain through a series of sinuses that connect to the jugular veins.
5b5d7b8ec12ba5c33733.alt: This diagram shows a lateral view of the brain and labels the location of the different sinuses.
5b5d7b8ec12ba5c33733.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

4ef58bb2a85419d3fcf6.title: The Cranial Nerves
4ef58bb2a85419d3fcf6.caption: The anatomical arrangement of the roots of the cranial nerves observed from an inferior view of the brain.
4ef58bb2a85419d3fcf6.alt: This diagrams shows the brain and the main nerves in the brain are labeled.
4ef58bb2a85419d3fcf6.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

a527b01877874971f32a.title: Segregation of Visual Field Information at the Optic Chiasm
a527b01877874971f32a.caption: Contralateral visual field information from the lateral retina projects to the ipsilateral brain, whereas ipsilateral visual field information has to decussate at the optic chiasm to reach the opposite side of the brain. (Note that this is an inferior view.)
a527b01877874971f32a.alt: This image shows the right and left visual fields in the brain. It describes how the optical fields map to different sides of the brain.
a527b01877874971f32a.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

7402b1f3d4192f1fcdc9.title: Vestibulo-ocular Reflex
7402b1f3d4192f1fcdc9.caption: Connections between the vestibular system and the cranial nerves controlling eye movement keep the eyes centered on a visual stimulus, even though the head is moving. During head movement, the eye muscles move the eyes in the opposite direction as the head movement, keeping the visual stimulus centered in the field of view.
7402b1f3d4192f1fcdc9.alt: This image shows how the excitation of eye muscles on one side, the inhibition of these muscles on the other side, and the compensating eye movements work together in vestibular ocular reflex.
7402b1f3d4192f1fcdc9.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

76db089a1e50517cbbb7.title: Nerve Plexuses of the Body
76db089a1e50517cbbb7.caption: There are four main nerve plexuses in the human body. The cervical plexus supplies nerves to the posterior head and neck, as well as to the diaphragm. The brachial plexus supplies nerves to the arm. The lumbar plexus supplies nerves to the anterior leg. The sacral plexus supplies nerves to the posterior leg.
76db089a1e50517cbbb7.alt: This figure shows a torso of a human body. The spinal cord is shown in the body and the main nerves along the spinal cord are labeled.
76db089a1e50517cbbb7.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

4a6cb18fdbea654f034e.title: Brodmann's Areas of the Cerebral Cortex
4a6cb18fdbea654f034e.caption: Brodmann mapping of functionally distinct regions of the cortex was based on its cytoarchitecture at a microscopic level.
4a6cb18fdbea654f034e.alt: In this figure, the Brodmann areas, identifying the functional regions of the brain, are mapped. The left panel shows the lateral surface of the brain and the right panel shows the medial surface.
4a6cb18fdbea654f034e.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

4ee355c537f8796bb286.title: Circle of Willis
4ee355c537f8796bb286.caption: The blood supply to the brain enters through the internal carotid arteries and the vertebral arteries, eventually giving rise to the circle of Willis.
4ee355c537f8796bb286.alt: This diagram shows a series of interconnected blood vessels and capillaries.
4ee355c537f8796bb286.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

13f1308a30ddb2b4af4e.title: Human Neuraxis
13f1308a30ddb2b4af4e.caption: The mammalian nervous system is arranged with the neural tube running along an anterior to posterior axis, from nose to tail for a four-legged animal like a dog. Humans, as two-legged animals, have a bend in the neuraxis between the brain stem and the diencephalon, along with a bend in the neck, so that the eyes and the face are oriented forward.
13f1308a30ddb2b4af4e.alt: This figure shows the neuroaxis in a human being in the left panel and a dog in the right panel.
13f1308a30ddb2b4af4e.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

e7ddc3b0d9e5b7bc4de1.title: Receptor Classification by Cell Type
e7ddc3b0d9e5b7bc4de1.caption: Receptor cell types can be classified on the basis of their structure. Sensory neurons can have either (a) free nerve endings or (b) encapsulated endings. Photoreceptors in the eyes, such as rod cells, are examples of (c) specialized receptor cells. These cells release neurotransmitters onto a bipolar cell, which then synapses with the optic nerve neurons.
e7ddc3b0d9e5b7bc4de1.alt: This figure shows the different types of receptors. The top panel shows a neuron receptor with free receptor endings, the middle panel shows a neuron receptor with encapsulated nerve endings, and the bottom panel shows a specialized receptor cell.
e7ddc3b0d9e5b7bc4de1.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

772d207d8a1f2afefcfb.title: Too Hot to Touch
772d207d8a1f2afefcfb.caption: When high temperature is sensed in the skin, a reflexive withdrawal is initiated by the muscles of the arm. Sensory neurons are activated by a stimulus, which is sent to the central nervous system, and a motor response is sent out to the skeletal muscles that control this movement.
772d207d8a1f2afefcfb.alt: This photo shows a red hot electric stove top.
772d207d8a1f2afefcfb.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

443fe084ca98a5a81972.title: Position of the Heart in the Thorax
443fe084ca98a5a81972.caption: The heart is located within the thoracic cavity, medially between the lungs in the mediastinum. It is about the size of a fist, is broad at the top, and tapers toward the base.
443fe084ca98a5a81972.alt: This diagram shows the location of the heart in the thorax.
443fe084ca98a5a81972.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

0d094680c541e01ed57b.title: Blood Flow from the Left Atrium to the Left Ventricle
0d094680c541e01ed57b.caption: (a) A transverse section through the heart illustrates the four heart valves. The two atrioventricular valves are open; the two semilunar valves are closed. The atria and vessels have been removed. (b) A frontal section through the heart illustrates blood flow through the mitral valve. When the mitral valve is open, it allows blood to move from the left atrium to the left ventricle. The aortic semilunar valve is closed to prevent backflow of blood from the aorta to the left ventricle.
0d094680c541e01ed57b.alt: The left panel of this figure shows the anterior view of the heart with the different valves, and the right panel of this figure shows the location of the mitral valve in the open position in the heart.
0d094680c541e01ed57b.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

228624219ea39c3f7411.title: Blood Flow from the Left Ventricle into the Great Vessels
228624219ea39c3f7411.caption: (a) A transverse section through the heart illustrates the four heart valves during ventricular contraction. The two atrioventricular valves are closed, but the two semilunar valves are open. The atria and vessels have been removed. (b) A frontal view shows the closed mitral (bicuspid) valve that prevents backflow of blood into the left atrium. The aortic semilunar valve is open to allow blood to be ejected into the aorta.
228624219ea39c3f7411.alt: The left panel of this figure shows the anterior view of the heart with the different valves, and the right panel of this figure shows the location of the mitral valve in the closed position in the heart.
228624219ea39c3f7411.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

c094ee7adff2f2ae75b7.title: Cardiac Conduction
c094ee7adff2f2ae75b7.caption: (1) The sinoatrial (SA) node and the remainder of the conduction system are at rest. (2) The SA node initiates the action potential, which sweeps across the atria. (3) After reaching the atrioventricular node, there is a delay of approximately 100 ms that allows the atria to complete pumping blood before the impulse is transmitted to the atrioventricular bundle. (4) Following the delay, the impulse travels through the atrioventricular bundle and bundle branches to the Purkinje fibers, and also reaches the right papillary muscle via the moderator band. (5) The impulse spreads to the contractile fibers of the ventricle. (6) Ventricular contraction begins.
c094ee7adff2f2ae75b7.alt: This image shows the different stages in the conduction cycle of the heart.
c094ee7adff2f2ae75b7.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

f5fac6a9b82c4e96c7a5.title: Dual System of the Human Blood Circulation
f5fac6a9b82c4e96c7a5.caption: Blood flows from the right atrium to the right ventricle, where it is pumped into the pulmonary circuit. The blood in the pulmonary artery branches is low in oxygen but relatively high in carbon dioxide. Gas exchange occurs in the pulmonary capillaries (oxygen into the blood, carbon dioxide out), and blood high in oxygen and low in carbon dioxide is returned to the left atrium. From here, blood enters the left ventricle, which pumps it into the systemic circuit. Following exchange in the systemic capillaries (oxygen and nutrients out of the capillaries and carbon dioxide and wastes in), blood returns to the right atrium and the cycle is repeated.
f5fac6a9b82c4e96c7a5.alt: The top panel shows the human heart with the arteries and veins labeled. The bottom panel shows the human circulatory system.
f5fac6a9b82c4e96c7a5.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

38808d98c7793805eda9.title: Differences in Ventricular Muscle Thickness
38808d98c7793805eda9.caption: The myocardium in the left ventricle is significantly thicker than that of the right ventricle. Both ventricles pump the same amount of blood, but the left ventricle must generate a much greater pressure to overcome greater resistance in the systemic circuit. The ventricles are shown in both relaxed and contracting states. Note the differences in the relative size of the lumens, the region inside each ventricle where the blood is contained.
38808d98c7793805eda9.alt: In this figure the left panel shows the muscles of the heart in the relaxed position, and the right panel shows the muscles of the heart in contracted position.
38808d98c7793805eda9.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

b753a14e1b10e6f45035.title: Heart Musculature
b753a14e1b10e6f45035.caption: The swirling pattern of cardiac muscle tissue contributes significantly to the heart’s ability to pump blood effectively.
b753a14e1b10e6f45035.alt: This diagram shows the muscles in the heart.
b753a14e1b10e6f45035.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

ae16293b245d77c3cf02.title: Pericardial Membranes and Layers of the Heart Wall
ae16293b245d77c3cf02.caption: The pericardial membrane that surrounds the heart consists of three layers and the pericardial cavity. The heart wall also consists of three layers. The pericardial membrane and the heart wall share the epicardium.
ae16293b245d77c3cf02.alt: This image shows a magnified view of the structure of the heart wall.
ae16293b245d77c3cf02.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

023c32619b3669c918a3.title: Congenital Heart Defects
023c32619b3669c918a3.caption: (a) A patent foramen ovale defect is an abnormal opening in the interatrial septum, or more commonly, a failure of the foramen ovale to close. (b) Coarctation of the aorta is an abnormal narrowing of the aorta. (c) A patent ductus arteriosus is the failure of the ductus arteriosus to close. (d) Tetralogy of Fallot includes an abnormal opening in the interventricular septum.
023c32619b3669c918a3.alt: This diagram shows the structure of the heart with different congenital defects. The top left panel shows patent foramen ovale, the top right panel shows coarctation of the aorta, the bottom left panel shows patent ductus ateriosus and the bottom right shows tetralogy of fallot.
023c32619b3669c918a3.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

a47a1417bca0a29b588a.title: Heart Valves
a47a1417bca0a29b588a.caption: With the atria and major vessels removed, all four valves are clearly visible, although it is difficult to distinguish the three separate cusps of the tricuspid valve.
a47a1417bca0a29b588a.alt: This diagram shows the anterior view of the heart with the different heart valves labeled.
a47a1417bca0a29b588a.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

6829cfea192becc42a68.title: Coronary Circulation
6829cfea192becc42a68.caption: The anterior view of the heart shows the prominent coronary surface vessels. The posterior view of the heart shows the prominent coronary surface vessels.
6829cfea192becc42a68.alt: The top panel of this figure shows the anterior view of the heart while the bottom panel shows the posterior view of the heart. The different blood vessels are labeled.
6829cfea192becc42a68.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

9ea6a267ebc827ab1826.title: Atherosclerotic Coronary Arteries
9ea6a267ebc827ab1826.caption: In this coronary angiogram (X-ray), the dye makes visible two occluded coronary arteries. Such blockages can lead to decreased blood flow (ischemia) and insufficient oxygen (hypoxia) delivered to the cardiac tissues. If uncorrected, this can lead to cardiac muscle death (myocardial infarction).
9ea6a267ebc827ab1826.alt: This photo shows a blockage in the coronary artery and in the circumflex artery.
9ea6a267ebc827ab1826.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

2e631db3847765b96d9f.title: Action Potential in Cardiac Contractile Cells
2e631db3847765b96d9f.caption: (a) Note the long plateau phase due to the influx of calcium ions. The extended refractory period allows the cell to fully contract before another electrical event can occur. (b) The action potential for heart muscle is compared to that of skeletal muscle.
2e631db3847765b96d9f.alt: The top panel of this figure shows millivolts as a function of time with the various stages labeled. The bottom left panel shows action potential and tension as a function of time for skeletal muscle, and the bottom right panel shows the action potential and tension as a function of time for cardiac muscle.
2e631db3847765b96d9f.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

6ee6ac5fad0cc6223eb0.title: Conduction System of the Heart
6ee6ac5fad0cc6223eb0.caption: Specialized conducting components of the heart include the sinoatrial node, the internodal pathways, the atrioventricular node, the atrioventricular bundle, the right and left bundle branches, and the Purkinje fibers.
6ee6ac5fad0cc6223eb0.alt: This image shows the anterior view of the frontal section of the heart with the major parts labeled.
6ee6ac5fad0cc6223eb0.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

1ee0bb02e59190d42e5f.title: Autonomic Innervation of the Heart
1ee0bb02e59190d42e5f.caption: Cardioaccelerator and cardioinhibitory areas are components of the paired cardiac centers located in the medulla oblongata of the brain. They innervate the heart via sympathetic cardiac nerves that increase cardiac activity and vagus (parasympathetic) nerves that slow cardiac activity.
1ee0bb02e59190d42e5f.alt: This figure shows the brain and the nerves connecting the brain to the heart.
1ee0bb02e59190d42e5f.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

2cb728cceb221a4af5c7.title: Effects of Parasympathetic and Sympathetic Stimulation on Normal Sinus Rhythm
2cb728cceb221a4af5c7.caption: The wave of depolarization in a normal sinus rhythm shows a stable resting HR. Following parasympathetic stimulation, HR slows. Following sympathetic stimulation, HR increases.
2cb728cceb221a4af5c7.alt: This figure shows three graphs. The top panel shows the normal or resting potential with time. The middle panel shows membrane potential with time in a parasympathetic stimulation where the heart rate is decreased. The bottom panel shows membrane potential with time in a sympathetic stimulation with increased heart rate.
2cb728cceb221a4af5c7.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

7a059885e31be254d4f4.title: Common ECG Abnormalities
7a059885e31be254d4f4.caption: (a) In a second-degree or partial block, one-half of the P waves are not followed by the QRS complex and T waves while the other half are. (b) In atrial fibrillation, the electrical pattern is abnormal prior to the QRS complex, and the frequency between the QRS complexes has increased. (c) In ventricular tachycardia, the shape of the QRS complex is abnormal. (d) In ventricular fibrillation, there is no normal electrical activity. (e) In a third-degree block, there is no correlation between atrial activity (the P wave) and ventricular activity (the QRS complex).
7a059885e31be254d4f4.alt: In this image the QT cycle for different heart conditions are shown. From top to bottom, the arrhythmias shown are second-degree partial block, atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation and third degree block.
7a059885e31be254d4f4.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

8724312e0aad2b5d9a6b.title: Electrocardiogram
8724312e0aad2b5d9a6b.caption: A normal tracing shows the P wave, QRS complex, and T wave. Also indicated are the PR, QT, QRS, and ST intervals, plus the P-R and S-T segments.
8724312e0aad2b5d9a6b.alt: This figure shows a graph of millivolts over time and the heart cycles during an ECG.
8724312e0aad2b5d9a6b.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

9b5092a05edc8b192bc8.title: Relationship between the Cardiac Cycle and ECG
9b5092a05edc8b192bc8.caption: Initially, both the atria and ventricles are relaxed (diastole). The P wave represents depolarization of the atria and is followed by atrial contraction (systole). Atrial systole extends until the QRS complex, at which point, the atria relax. The QRS complex represents depolarization of the ventricles and is followed by ventricular contraction. The T wave represents the repolarization of the ventricles and marks the beginning of ventricular relaxation.
9b5092a05edc8b192bc8.alt: This image shows the correlation between the cardiac cycle and the different stages in a electrocardiogram.
9b5092a05edc8b192bc8.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

d37af070b52b30b52358.title: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle
d37af070b52b30b52358.caption: In this illustration, the x-axis reflects time with a recording of the heart sounds. The y-axis represents pressure.
d37af070b52b30b52358.alt: This image shows a graph of the blood pressure with the different stages labeled. Under the graph, a line shows the different sounds made by the beating heart.
d37af070b52b30b52358.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

cdb1cc30778b838f3188.title: Major Factors Influencing Cardiac Output
cdb1cc30778b838f3188.caption: Cardiac output is influenced by heart rate and stroke volume, both of which are also variable.
cdb1cc30778b838f3188.alt: This figure lists the different factors affecting the heart rate and stroke volume. It also shows how they both affect the cardiac output.
cdb1cc30778b838f3188.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

6998c683306781cf5a85.title: Major Factors Influencing Stroke Volume
6998c683306781cf5a85.caption: Multiple factors impact preload, afterload, and contractility, and are the major considerations influencing SV.
6998c683306781cf5a85.alt: This table describes major factors influencing stroke volume. Preload may be raised due to longer filling time or increased venous return. These factors increase end diastolic volume and increase stroke volume. Preload may be lowered due to decreased thyroid hormones, decreased calcium ions, high or low potassium ions, high or low sodium, low body temperature, hypoxia, abnormal pH balance, or drugs (for example, calcium channel blockers). These factors decrease end diastolic volume and decrease stroke volume. Contractility may be raised due to sympathetic stimulation, epinephrine and norepinephrine, high intracellular calcium ions, high blood calcium level, thyroid hormones, or glucagon. These factors decrease end systolic volume and increase stroke volume. Contractility may be lowered due to parasympathetic stimulation, acetylcholine, hypoxia, or hyperkalemia. These factors increase end systolic volume and decrease stroke volume. Afterload may be raised due to increased vascular resistance or semilunar valve damage. These factors increase end systolic volume and decrease stroke volume. Afterload may be lowered due to decreased vascular resistance. This factor decreases end systolic volume and increases stroke volume.
6998c683306781cf5a85.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

8b367e48518c876a8e33.title: Action Potential at the SA Node
8b367e48518c876a8e33.caption: The prepotential is due to a slow influx of sodium ions until the threshold is reached followed by a rapid depolarization and repolarization. The prepotential accounts for the membrane reaching threshold and initiates the spontaneous depolarization and contraction of the cell. Note the lack of a resting potential.
8b367e48518c876a8e33.alt: This graph shows the change in membrane potential as a function of time.
8b367e48518c876a8e33.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

a318632388714858234a.title: Layers of the Alimentary Canal
a318632388714858234a.caption: The wall of the alimentary canal has four basic tissue layers: the mucosa, submucosa, muscularis, and serosa.
a318632388714858234a.alt: This image shows the cross section of the alimentary canal. The different layers of the alimentary canal are shown as concentric cylinders with major muscles and veins labeled.
a318632388714858234a.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

7df47442006d68a795e1.title: Digestive Processes
7df47442006d68a795e1.caption: The digestive processes are ingestion, propulsion, mechanical digestion, chemical digestion, absorption, and defecation.
7df47442006d68a795e1.alt: This image shows the different processes involved in digestion. The image shows how food travels from the mouth through the major organs. Associated textboxes list the different processes such as propulsion, chemical and mechanical digestion and absorption near the organs where they take place.
7df47442006d68a795e1.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

da2e3b30e7e372070208.title: Peristalsis
da2e3b30e7e372070208.caption: Peristalsis moves food through the digestive tract with alternating waves of muscle contraction and relaxation.
da2e3b30e7e372070208.alt: This image shows the peristaltic movement of food. In the left image, the food bolus is towards the top of the esophagus and arrows pointing downward show the direction of movement of the peristaltic wave. In the center image, the food bolus and the wave movement are closer to the center of the esophagus and in the right image, the bolus and the wave are close to the bottom end of the esophagus.
da2e3b30e7e372070208.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

545e4e15019ec6e9e031.title: Segmentation
545e4e15019ec6e9e031.caption: Segmentation separates chyme and then pushes it back together, mixing it and providing time for digestion and absorption.
545e4e15019ec6e9e031.alt: This diagram shows the process of segmentation in the intestines. The left panel shows the separation of chime, the middle panel shows the remixing of the chime by pushing it back together and the right panel indicates that the chime is being digested and absorbed.
545e4e15019ec6e9e031.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

a2c27f99d30539f13ca7.title: Digestive Secretions and Absorption of Water
a2c27f99d30539f13ca7.caption: Absorption is a complex process, in which nutrients from digested food are harvested.
a2c27f99d30539f13ca7.alt: This image shows the human digestive system. Next to each organ, a text callout identifies how water and digestive secretions such as saliva and bile are processed.
a2c27f99d30539f13ca7.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

32c814b50a8d86b9d416.title: Stomach
32c814b50a8d86b9d416.caption: The stomach has four major regions: the cardia, fundus, body, and pylorus. The addition of an inner oblique smooth muscle layer gives the muscularis the ability to vigorously churn and mix food.
32c814b50a8d86b9d416.alt: This image shows a cross-section of the stomach, and the major parts: the cardia, fundus, body and pylorus are labeled.
32c814b50a8d86b9d416.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

81d145c36b90d434b47e.title: Digestive Enzymes and Hormones
81d145c36b90d434b47e.caption: Enzymes in the stomach and small intestine break down proteins into amino acids. HCl in the stomach aids in proteolysis, and hormones secreted by intestinal cells direct the digestive processes.
81d145c36b90d434b47e.alt: The left panel shows the main organs of the digestive system, and the right panel shows a magnified view of the intestine. Text callouts indicate the different protein digesting enzymes produced in different organs.
81d145c36b90d434b47e.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

553df4103fde72346610.title: Digestion and Absorption
553df4103fde72346610.caption: Digestion begins in the mouth and continues as food travels through the small intestine. Most absorption occurs in the small intestine.
553df4103fde72346610.alt: This diagram identifies the functions of mechanical and chemical digestion and absorption at each organ. Next to each organ, a callout identifies which steps of digestion take place in that particular organ.
553df4103fde72346610.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

5971fa5ca87b4027c5a9.title: Structure of ATP Molecule
5971fa5ca87b4027c5a9.caption: Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) is the energy molecule of the cell. During catabolic reactions, ATP is created and energy is stored until needed during anabolic reactions.
5971fa5ca87b4027c5a9.alt: This diagram shows the chemical structure of adenosine triphosphate, and how different reactions add or remove phosphate groups.
5971fa5ca87b4027c5a9.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

465731f09d40e2bf5ad8.title: The Peritoneum
465731f09d40e2bf5ad8.caption: A cross-section of the abdomen shows the relationship between abdominal organs and the peritoneum (darker lines).

0880ee529f2a132ea69c.title: Accessory Organs
0880ee529f2a132ea69c.caption: The liver, pancreas, and gallbladder are considered accessory digestive organs, but their roles in the digestive system are vital.
0880ee529f2a132ea69c.alt: This diagram shows the accessory organs of the digestive system. The liver, spleen, pancreas, gallbladder and their major parts are shown.

41e584ea1d16242aed02.title: Tongue

41e584ea1d16242aed02.alt: This diagram shows the structure of the tongue and different parts of the tongue are labeled.
41e584ea1d16242aed02.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

0bc890d10f1e3d5fd278.title: Permanent and Deciduous Teeth
0bc890d10f1e3d5fd278.caption: This figure of two human dentitions shows the arrangement of teeth in the maxilla and mandible, and the relationship between the deciduous and permanent teeth.
0bc890d10f1e3d5fd278.alt: This diagram shows the arrangement of permanent and deciduous teeth in human. The permanent teeth are labeled along with the average age at which they emerge. An inset shows the arrangement of the deciduous teeth, with the age at which they emerge listed.

06bce4d687ea311ab804.title: Salivary glands
06bce4d687ea311ab804.caption: The major salivary glands are located outside the oral mucosa and deliver saliva into the mouth through ducts.

06bce4d687ea311ab804.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

17e370daa011b4826119.title: Pharynx
17e370daa011b4826119.caption: The pharynx runs from the nostrils to the esophagus and the larynx.

c241447f395e3bb4aa26.title: Deglutition
c241447f395e3bb4aa26.caption: Deglutition includes the voluntary phase and two involuntary phases: the pharyngeal phase and the esophageal phase.

f9f915213533d0a3e960.title: Histology of the Stomach

The gastric glands (one gland is shown enlarged on the right) contain different types of cells that secrete a variety of enzymes, including hydrochloride acid, which activates the protein-digesting enzyme pepsin.

78f2da45cafc2ba2d038.caption: The three regions of the small intestine are the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum.
78f2da45cafc2ba2d038.alt: This diagram shows the small intestine. The different parts of the small intestine are labeled.

dc6fd2bf1ea8c4a72067.title: Exocrine and Endocrine Pancreas
dc6fd2bf1ea8c4a72067.caption: The pancreas has a head, a body, and a tail. It delivers pancreatic juice to the duodenum through the pancreatic duct.

43ee32da0211be818d4a.title: Large Intestine

b6cd41d2aeb74b091c28.title: The Three Phases of Gastric Secretion
b6cd41d2aeb74b091c28.caption: Gastric secretion occurs in three phases: cephalic, gastric, and intestinal. During each phase, the secretion of gastric juice can be stimulated or inhibited.
b6cd41d2aeb74b091c28.alt: This flowchart shows the three different phases of gastric secretion. The top panel shows the cephalic phase, the middle panel shows the gastric phase and the bottom panel shows the intestinal phase.

58407d648910140c4749.title: Lipid Metabolism
58407d648910140c4749.caption: Lipids may follow one of several pathways during metabolism. Glycerol and fatty acids follow different pathways.

4024ebb4c621dff602a6.title: Teniae Coli, Haustra, and Epiploic Appendages
4024ebb4c621dff602a6.alt: This image shows the Taenia Coli, haustra and epiploic appendages, which are parts of the large intestine.

fcda18a635dc699f7e05.title: Microscopic Anatomy of the Liver
fcda18a635dc699f7e05.caption: The liver receives oxygenated blood from the hepatic artery and nutrient-rich deoxygenated blood from the hepatic portal vein.
fcda18a635dc699f7e05.alt: This image shows the microscopic anatomy of the liver. The top panel shows the liver; the center panel shows a magnified view of the connective tissue and the lobules. The bottom panel shows a further magnified view of a lobule, identifying the veins, bile duct and the sinusoids.
fcda18a635dc699f7e05.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

fd6efa9b5efe9fedc4ab.title: Absorptive State
fd6efa9b5efe9fedc4ab.caption: During the absorptive state, the body digests food and absorbs the nutrients.
fd6efa9b5efe9fedc4ab.alt: This figure shows how nutrients are absorbed by the body. The diagram shows digested nutrients entering the blood stream and being absorbed by liver cells, muscle cells, and adipose cells. Underneath each panel, text details the process taking place in each cell type.

548f49e4ffbb6dc7061a.title: Gallbladder
548f49e4ffbb6dc7061a.caption: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile, and releases it into the two-way cystic duct when it is needed by the small intestine.
548f49e4ffbb6dc7061a.alt: This figure shows the gallbladder and its major parts are labeled.
548f49e4ffbb6dc7061a.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

edb9afc7a2d716c8c0c8.title: Energy from Amino Acids
edb9afc7a2d716c8c0c8.caption: Amino acids can be broken down into precursors for glycolysis or the Krebs cycle. Amino acids (in bold) can enter the cycle through more than one pathway.
edb9afc7a2d716c8c0c8.alt: This figure  shows the different reactions in which products of carbohydrate breakdown are converted into different amino acids.
edb9afc7a2d716c8c0c8.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

71cd69877156bd7fb84e.title: Triglyceride Broken Down into a Monoglyceride
71cd69877156bd7fb84e.caption: A triglyceride molecule (a) breaks down into a monoglyceride (b).
71cd69877156bd7fb84e.alt: The top image shows the chemical formula for a triglyceride, and the bottom panel shows the formula for a monoglyceride.
71cd69877156bd7fb84e.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

d41aee55f7eb47928cf0.title: Carbohydrate Digestion Flow Chart
d41aee55f7eb47928cf0.caption: Carbohydrates are broken down into their monomers in a series of steps.
d41aee55f7eb47928cf0.alt: This flow chart shows the steps in digestion of carbohydrates. The different levels shown are starch and glycogen, disaccharides and monosaccharides. Under each type of sugar, examples and the enzymes responsible for digestion are listed.
d41aee55f7eb47928cf0.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

22068b30d4daabe5d1aa.title: Lipid Absorption
22068b30d4daabe5d1aa.caption: Unlike amino acids and simple sugars, lipids are transformed as they are absorbed through epithelial cells.
22068b30d4daabe5d1aa.alt: This diagram shows how lipids are absorbed from the lumen of the intestine into the lacteals. The fatty acid micelles are shown to enter the epithelial cell and form chylomicrons inside the Golgi apparatus. Then, the chylomicrons are extruded from the epithelial cell and are taken up by the lacteals.
22068b30d4daabe5d1aa.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

22799592e8598bf23a40.title: Ketogenesis
22799592e8598bf23a40.caption: Excess acetyl CoA is diverted from the Krebs cycle to the ketogenesis pathway. This reaction occurs in the mitochondria of liver cells. The result is the production of β-hydroxybutyrate, the primary ketone body found in the blood.
22799592e8598bf23a40.alt: This pathway shows the production of beta-hydroxybutyrate from acetyl-CoA.
22799592e8598bf23a40.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

4fb118bcaebf53d07e05.title: Binding of Lipid-Soluble Hormones
4fb118bcaebf53d07e05.caption: A steroid hormone directly initiates the production of proteins within a target cell. Steroid hormones easily diffuse through the cell membrane. The hormone binds to its receptor in the cytosol, forming a receptor–hormone complex. The receptor–hormone complex then enters the nucleus and binds to the target gene on the DNA. Transcription of the gene creates a messenger RNA that is translated into the desired protein within the cytoplasm.
4fb118bcaebf53d07e05.alt: This illustration shows the steps involved with the binding of lipid-soluble hormones. Lipid-soluble hormones, such as steroid hormones, easily diffuse through the cell membrane. The hormone binds to its receptor in the cytosol, forming a receptor-hormone complex. The receptor-hormone complex then enters the nucleus and binds to the target gene on the cell’s DNA. Transcription of the gene creates a messenger RNA that is translated into the desired protein within the cytoplasm. It is these proteins that alter the cell’s activity.
4fb118bcaebf53d07e05.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

8b37531ce29ab7e805d1.title: Amine, Peptide, Protein, and Steroid Hormone Structure
8b37531ce29ab7e805d1.alt: This table shows the chemical structure of amine hormones, peptide hormones, protein hormones, and steroid hormones. Amine hormones are amino acids with modified side groups. The example given is norepinephrine, which contains the NH two group typical of an amino acid, along with a hydroxyl (OH) group. The carboxyl group typical of most amino acids is replaced with a benzene ring, depicted as a hexagon of carbons that are connected by alternating single and double bonds. Peptide hormones are composed of short chains of amino acids. The example given is oxytocin, which has a chain of the following amino acids: GLY, LEU, PRO. The PRO is the bottom of the chain, which connects to a ring of the following amino acids: CYS, CYS, TYR, ILE, GLU, and ASP. Protein hormones are composed of long chains of linked amino acids. The example given is human growth hormone, which is composed of a bundle of amino acid strands, some thread-like, some coiled, and some in flat, folded sheets. Finally, steroid hormones are derived from the lipid cholesterol. Testosterone and progesterone are given as examples, which each contain several hexagonal and pentagonal carbon rings linked together.
8b37531ce29ab7e805d1.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

127c1e274719a27fe134.title: Binding of Water-Soluble Hormones
127c1e274719a27fe134.caption: Water-soluble hormones cannot diffuse through the cell membrane. These hormones must bind to a surface cell-membrane receptor. The receptor then initiates a cell-signaling pathway within the cell involving G proteins, adenylyl cyclase, the secondary messenger cyclic AMP (cAMP), and protein kinases. In the final step, these protein kinases phosphorylate proteins in the cytoplasm. This activates proteins in the cell that carry out the changes specified by the hormone.
127c1e274719a27fe134.alt: This illustration shows the binding of water-soluble hormones. Water-soluble hormones cannot diffuse through the cell membrane. These hormones must bind to a receptor on the outer surface of the cell membrane. The receptor then activates a G protein in the cytoplasm, which travels to and activates adenylyl cyclase. Adenylyl cyclase catalyzes the conversion of ATP to CAMP, the secondary messenger in this pathway. CAMP, in turn, activates protein kinases, which phosphorylate proteins in the cytoplasm. This phosphorylation, shown as a P being added to a polypeptide chain, activates the proteins, allowing them to alter cell activity.
127c1e274719a27fe134.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

a54cba495794b2be4e81.title: Classic Negative Feedback Loop
a54cba495794b2be4e81.caption: A classic negative feedback loop controls the regulation of thyroid hormone levels.
a54cba495794b2be4e81.alt: This diagram illustrates a negative feedback loop. It shows the general steps of a negative feedback loop at the center (imbalance, hormone release, correction, and negative feedback) using the example of the hormone cascade that regulates metabolic rate. The hypothalamus releases TRH in response to low metabolic rate and or low T three and T four concentrations in the blood (imbalance). This triggers TSH release by the pituitary (hormone release). The TSH travels to the thyroid where it triggers T three and T four release by the thyroid cells. T three and T four increase basal metabolic rate of the body cells and cause a rise in body temperature (the calorigenic effect). T three and T four then feed back to the hypothalamus and inhibits TRH and TSH release. If metabolic rate is high and or T three and T four concentrations are low, then the hypothalamus stops releasing TRH (negative feedback). As a result, the anterior pituitary will not release TSH and no T three or T four will be produced by the thyroid.
a54cba495794b2be4e81.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

2c44dfbbad90124e0971.title: Hypothalamus–Pituitary Complex
2c44dfbbad90124e0971.caption: The hypothalamus region lies inferior and anterior to the thalamus. It connects to the pituitary gland by the stalk-like infundibulum. The pituitary gland consists of an anterior and posterior lobe, with each lobe secreting different hormones in response to signals from the hypothalamus.
2c44dfbbad90124e0971.alt: This illustration shows the hypothalamus-pituitary complex, which is located at the base of the brain and shown here from a lateral view. The hypothalamus lies inferior and anterior to the thalamus, which is sits atop the brainstem. The hypothalamus connects to the pituitary gland by the stalk-like infundibulum. The pituitary gland looks like a sac containing two balls hanging from the infundibulum. The “balls” are the anterior and posterior lobes of the pituitary. Each lobe secretes different hormones in response to signals from the hypothalamus.
2c44dfbbad90124e0971.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

0e5e2b1a1f87ebb1b82f.title: Anterior Pituitary
0e5e2b1a1f87ebb1b82f.caption: The anterior pituitary manufactures seven hormones. The hypothalamus produces separate hormones that stimulate or inhibit hormone production in the anterior pituitary. Hormones from the hypothalamus reach the anterior pituitary via the hypophyseal portal system.
0e5e2b1a1f87ebb1b82f.alt: This illustration zooms in on the hypothalamus and the attached pituitary gland. The anterior pituitary is highlighted. Three neurosecretory cells are secreting hormones into a web-like network of arteries within the infundibulum. The artery net is labeled the primary capillary plexus of the hypophyseal portal system. The superior hypophysel artery enters the primary capillary plexus from outside of the infundibulum. The hypophyseal portal vein runs down from the primary capillary plexus, through the infundibulum, and connects to the secondary capillary plexus of the hypophyseal portal system. The secondary capillary plexus is located within the anterior pituitary. The hormones released from the neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus travel through the primary capillary plexus, down the hypophyseal portal vein, and into the secondary capillary plexus. There, the hypothalamus hormones stimulate the anterior pituitary to release its hormones. The anterior pituitary hormones leave the primary capillary plexus from a single vein at the bottom of the anterior lobe.
0e5e2b1a1f87ebb1b82f.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

2ee8f8d4a4d53aed6160.title: Posterior Pituitary
2ee8f8d4a4d53aed6160.caption: Neurosecretory cells in the hypothalamus release oxytocin (OT) or ADH into the posterior lobe of the pituitary gland. These hormones are stored or released into the blood via the capillary plexus.
2ee8f8d4a4d53aed6160.alt: This illustration zooms in on the hypothalamus and the attached pituitary gland. The posterior pituitary is highlighted. Two nuclei in the hypothalamus contain neurosecretory cells that release different hormones. The neurosecretory cells of the paraventricular nucleus release oxytocin (OT) while the neurosecretory cells of the supraoptic nucleus release anti-diuretic hormone (ADH). The neurosecretory cells stretch down the infundibulum into the posterior pituitary. The tube-like extensions of the neurosecretory cells within the infundibulum are labeled the hypothalamophypophyseal tracts. These tracts connect with a web-like network of blood vessels in the posterior pituitary called the capillary plexus. From the capillary plexus, the posterior pituitary secretes the OT or ADH into a single vein that exits the pituitary.
2ee8f8d4a4d53aed6160.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

f03a41c34b0a89d8f6ac.title: Negative Feedback Loop
f03a41c34b0a89d8f6ac.caption: The release of adrenal glucocorticoids is stimulated by the release of hormones from the hypothalamus and pituitary gland. This signaling is inhibited when glucocorticoid levels become elevated by causing negative signals to the pituitary gland and hypothalamus.
f03a41c34b0a89d8f6ac.alt: This diagram shows a negative feedback loop using the example of glucocorticoid regulation in the blood. Step 1 in the cycle is when an imbalance occurs. The hypothalamus perceives low blood concentrations of glucocorticoids in the blood. This is illustrated by there being only 5 glucocorticoids floating in a cross section of an artery. Step 2 in the cycle is hormone release, where the hypothalamus releases corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH). Step 3 is labeled correction. Here, the CRH release starts a hormone cascade that triggers the adrenal gland to release glucocorticoid into the blood. This allows the blood concentration of glucocorticoid to increase, as illustrated by 8 glucocorticoid molecules now being present in the cross section of the artery. Step 4 is labeled negative feedback. Here, the hypothalamus perceives normal concentrations of glucocorticoids in the blood and stops releasing CRH. This brings blood glucocorticoid levels back to homeostasis.
f03a41c34b0a89d8f6ac.credit: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology (release 1rc), CC BY 4.0.

c9747bfa29983c59b4b6.title: Parathyroid Hormone in Maintaining Blood Calcium Homeostasis
c9747bfa29983c59b4b6.caption: Parathyroid hormone increases blood calcium levels when they drop too low. Conversely, calcitonin, which is released from the thyroid gland, decreases blood calcium levels when they become too high. These two mechanisms constantly maintain blood calcium concentration at homeostasis.
c9747bfa29983c59b4b6.alt: This diagram shows the role of parathyroid hormone in maintaining blood calcium homeostasis. When blood calcium concentration drops, chief cells of the parathyroid gland release parathyroid hormone (PTH). PTH affects bone, the kidneys and the intestines. In regards to bone, PTH inhibits osteoblasts and stimulates osteoclasts. This results in compact bone being broken down, as illustrated by an osteoclast burrowing into the surface of a bone. The break down releases calcium ions into a nearby blood vessel. The osteoblasts are inactive in this stage.
